Speaking at a press briefing in Lagos to announce the activities of 2026 AFRIFF Week, Hannatu Musawa, Minister of Art, Culture and the Creative Economy, officially announced the launch of the 15th edition of the Africa International Film Festival.
Musawa, represented by Shaibu Husseini, director-general of the National Film and Video Censors Board (NFVCB), highlighted the festival’s decade-and-a-half milestone as a critical milestone for the continent’s entertainment industry, framing the creative economy as a major engine for economic growth.
“For fifteen years, AFRIFF has not merely been a date on our calendar — it has been a monument to African storytelling, a catalyst for economic growth within the creative sector, and a beacon that has been pushing local genius to the global stage,” Husseini said.
Central to this year’s festival theme, “Frames of the Future,” is a government commitment to modernize regulatory and support frameworks for local filmmakers.
The ministry confirmed it is actively reshaping federal policies to improve distribution infrastructure, spur tech adoption, and foster international co-productions. This key bottleneck has historically constrained monetization across the African film market.
She urged African creators to embrace cutting-edge production technology, novel storytelling methods, and cross-border partnerships to compete globally.
While laying out a forward-looking vision, she paid tribute to AFRIFF’s leadership and founding visionaries for sustaining institutional excellence and capacity building over 15 years.
Highlighting the festival’s surging international clout, Chioma Ude, AFRIFF founder and executive director, revealed that building on momentum from the Cannes Film Festival, where the festival was invited to host its prestigious La Fabrique Cinema program, AFRIFF has secured a major milestone for its 15th edition, securing a spot to feature through to the closing night of the premier global market.
Ude noted that while early deliberations focused on the disruptive role of artificial intelligence and emerging tech, initial programming data revealed a striking demographic shift: women directed and produced 85 percent of the feature films selected for this year’s screening lineup.
To bridge industry talk with operational execution, this year’s festival program will heavily emphasize targeted panels designed to resolve persistent financing bottlenecks, bringing together key dealmakers to establish clear pathways for project funding and execution across the continent.
The festival is also seeing a sharp surge in international interest, particularly from North American industry players, following last year’s record engagements; project financing discussions range from $5 million to over $20 million—a trend organisers attribute to aggressive global outreach and expanding market confidence.
Underscoring the growing role of private capital in scaling Nigeria’s creative economy, Joelle Haykal, group executive director of Mikano International Limited, said that corporate involvement must extend beyond traditional commercial sponsorship toward long-term local investment and brand building.
Haykal emphasized that operating in Nigeria carries a broader mandate to cultivate domestic talent and export the country’s economic and creative potential to global markets.
Advocating for responsible corporate citizenship, Haykal called on consumers and regulators to back enterprises that actively reinvest in national economic development, noting that corporate partnerships with platform drivers like AFRIFF are essential for building a resilient national economy. The festival is scheduled to take place in Lagos from November 1 to 7, 2026.
